common_name: Pink Shrimp Plant (Soft-Pink Bronze Shrimp Plant)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in average, well-drained soil; 'Pink' flowers almost continuously through the warm season and benefits from an early light feeding to push new growth.

directions: 'Pink' is a soft-colored sport of the familiar bronze shrimp plant, carrying the same arching, overlapping bracts but shaded in blush pink rather than the species' typical rust-red to bronze tones, with small white tubular true flowers peeking out from between the bracts. It roots readily from stem cuttings and establishes quickly in beds, borders, or large containers, flowering almost without interruption from spring through fall in warm climates and year-round where winters stay mild. Along the Gulf Coast it does best with morning sun and afternoon shade, since intense midday sun can bleach the delicate bract color and stress the foliage. Cut plants back hard in late winter or after a cold snap to renew compact, bushy growth and keep the long bloom spikes forming at a manageable height.

common_name: Katie Pink Mexican Petunia (Dwarf Pink-Flowered Ruellia)

planting.note: Divide or set out container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil; 'Katie Pink' spreads by rhizomes to form a dense low mat and blooms from early summer through fall.

directions: 'Katie Pink' is a light-pink-flowered counterpart to the well-known dwarf 'Katie' Mexican petunia, forming the same tidy, grassy-leaved 9-to-12-inch mound but opening clear pink, funnel-shaped flowers instead of purple-blue. Each flower lasts only a day, but the dense mounding habit produces a steady flush of new blooms from early summer into fall, making it a reliable low edger or container filler in Gulf Coast beds. It tolerates heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established, though it colors and flowers best with consistent moisture and full sun. Because Ruellia simplex is listed as a Category I invasive species by the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council, gardeners in Florida and other warm, humid regions should watch for self-sown seedlings nearby and consider confining plantings or choosing sterile cultivars where naturalized spread is a concern.

common_name: Southern Star Blue Mexican Petunia (Compact Seed-Grown Ruellia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50F; in zone 9 and warmer, 'Southern Star Blue' persists and spreads as a perennial.

directions: 'Southern Star Blue' is a compact, seed-propagated Mexican petunia bred for uniform bedding and container performance, bearing sky-blue, funnel-shaped flowers with a deeper blue throat over a tidy, well-branched mound well under knee height. Unlike cutting-grown landscape selections, it is marketed as F1 seed and finishes quickly from a spring sowing, flowering through summer heat and holding its compact habit without the legginess of older tall Ruellia types. It tolerates both standing moisture and short dry spells once established and shrugs off the heat and humidity typical of Gulf Coast summers. Where it is hardy as a perennial, watch for volunteer seedlings nearby, since Ruellia simplex in all its forms is classified as a Category I invasive species by the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council.
